steps.user_message: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Atlanta GA. W-2 from Pacific Software: $68,200. Additional income: $16,300 (freelance writing, 3 clients), $2,650 from Capital One 360, $670 from Merrill Edge. Home office: 170 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,880/month for 740 sq ft. Deductions: $5,100 student loan interest (Great Lakes, 2019–2021); $950 to Red Cross have the receipt; $1,050 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — I can walk you through this. I’ll explain what’s deductible, whether itemizing probably makes sense, how to treat the home office, what IRS forms you’ll use, and what I need from you to give exact numbers. I’ll also show quick rough calculations so you can see the likely impact.

Summary / quick answer
- You must report: W-2 wages ($68,200), freelance income ($16,300) on Schedule C, and interest/dividends ($2,650 + $670 = $3,320) on the 1040.
- Most likely it will be better to take the federal standard deduction unless your itemizable deductions (charity, state tax paid, mortgage interest, etc.) exceed the standard amount. From the data you gave (only $950 charitable shown), the standard deduction will probably be larger — but I can check if you tell me state tax withheld and any other deductible items.
- Home office: you can take a home‑office deduction for the 170 sq ft exclusive business space. You can choose either the simplified method (170 sq ft × $5 = $850) or the actual method (about 170/740 ≈ 22.97% of allowable home expenses such as rent, utilities, renter’s insurance, etc.). Use whichever gives the larger deduction, but the home‑office deduction for the actual method generally requires Form 8829.
- Student loan interest: the deduction is an “above‑the‑line” adjustment up to $2,500 (not $5,100). It phases out based on MAGI (single taxpayers phase out near the ~$75k–$90k range in recent years). I need to know whether the $5,100 you mentioned was interest paid in tax year 2024 and whether you have Form 1098‑E from Great Lakes.
- Unreimbursed expenses: if these $1,050 are expenses related to your self‑employment (freelance work), they are deductible on Schedule C. If they are unreimbursed employee expenses from your W‑2 job, they are not deductible for federal returns under current law (2018–2025 TCJA suspension).
- Forms you’ll need (federal): Form 1040, Schedule C (Profit/Loss from Business), Schedule SE (self‑employment tax), Form 8829 (if you use actual home‑office method), Form 8995/8995‑A (QBI deduction — possibly applicable), and Schedule 1 for adjustments (student loan interest, deductible part of self‑employment tax). Also attach any 1099‑NEC/1099‑MISC received, 1099‑INT (savings interest), 1099‑DIV or 1099‑B (brokerage), and Form 1098‑E for student loan interest if you have it. For state (Georgia) you’ll file GA Form 500 (check GA instructions for state itemizing vs standard).
- Also: pay attention to self‑employment tax (roughly 15.3% on net self‑employment income) and estimated tax payments for 2025 if you expect similar freelance income.

What I need / clarifying questions
1. Did you pay the $5,100 student‑loan interest during calendar year 2024, or is that the total interest charged over 2019–2021? (Only interest paid in 2024 can be deducted on your 2024 return.)
2. Are the $1,050 “unreimbursed expenses” business expenses for your freelance work, or expenses related to your W‑2 job (employee)? If W‑2 job expenses, they are not deductible on federal returns right now.
3. Do you have 1099‑NEC forms from your 3 clients, or will you need to report some income that did not generate a 1099? Do you have the 1099‑INT (Capital One 360) and brokerage 1099 (Merrill Edge)? These determine exactly how to report the $2,650 and $670 amounts (interest vs dividends/cap gains).
4. Do you pay utilities and renter’s insurance separately (and do you have amounts for annual utilities, internet, renter’s insurance)? If you want, provide annual totals and I’ll compute the actual home‑office allocation for you.
5. Any other deductible items not mentioned (state tax paid, property taxes, mortgage interest, large medical expenses, large unreimbursed charitable donations beyond the $950)?

Rough numbers and examples (illustrative)
Assumptions: student loan interest is eligible but limited to $2,500 (subject to phaseout); the $1,050 are business expenses for freelance work; you choose the actual home‑office method using only rent allocation (no utilities included for simplicity).

- Home office allocation: 170 / 740 = 22.97%.
- Annual rent = $1,880 × 12 = $22,560. Allocated share = 22.97% × $22,560 ≈ $5,188.
- If you include proportional utilities/insurance, add those amounts × 22.97% for a larger deduction.
- Simplified home‑office method: 170 × $5 = $850 (so actual (rent share) likely higher).
- Tentative Schedule C net income:
   - Gross freelance: $16,300
   - Less home‑office (actual example using rent share): −$5,188
   - Less other business expenses (your $1,050) : −$1,050
   - Net ≈ $10,062 (this is taxable business profit before self‑employment tax and QBI)
- Self‑employment tax (approx): net × 92.35% = taxable SE base → ≈ $9,295; SE tax at 15.3% ≈ $1,422. Half of that (~$711) is an adjustment to income on Schedule 1.
- QBI: you may be able to claim up to 20% of qualified business income (roughly 20% of the net from above, subject to limits), so that could reduce taxable income further. Form 8995 will be used if applicable.

Itemize vs standard
- Standard deduction for single taxpayers has been substantially larger since 2018. With only $950 of charitable donations listed and no mortgage interest mentioned, your itemized deductions are likely well below the standard deduction — so the standard deduction will probably be best.
- However, because the student loan interest deduction and the deductible half of SE tax reduce your AGI (above‑the‑line), they help regardless of whether you itemize.

Forms checklist (federal)
- Form 1040
- Schedule C (report freelance income & business expenses)
- Schedule SE (self‑employment tax)
- Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) if using the actual method; if you use simplified method, you don’t file Form 8829 for that deduction.
- Form 8995 or 8995‑A (QBI deduction) if eligible
- Schedule 1 (report adjustments including student loan interest up to $2,500 and deductible portion of SE tax)
- 1099‑NEC, 1099‑INT, 1099‑DIV/1099‑B, 1098‑E (keep them with your return)
- Georgia state return: GA Form 500 and any required state schedules

Other practical items & suggestions
- Keep receipts and a clear ledger for freelance expenses and home office costs (rent, utilities, internet).
- If you expect similar freelance income in 2025, consider making quarterly estimated tax payments to avoid underpayment penalties.
- Get Form 1098‑E from Great Lakes for the amount of student loan interest paid in 2024. If your MAGI is above the phaseout, the deduction may be reduced or disallowed.
- If you want, I can run precise calculations if you provide:
   • confirmation on student loan interest year / Form 1098‑E amount,
   • whether the $1,050 is freelance business expenses,
   • any annual utilities/internet/renter’s insurance amounts,
   • state tax withheld from your W‑2 or any other deductible state/local taxes paid.

Would you like me to:
- (A) calculate exact deductions and approximate federal tax with the numbers you have (I’ll make reasonable assumptions where needed), or
- (B) search for specific forms/instructions you need (IRS form links), or
- (C) walk you through completing Schedule C and Form 8829 step by step?

Tell me which and answer the clarifying questions above and I’ll run the numbers or produce form‑by‑form instructions.
